blueprint.speaker: A grown daughter, now middle-aged, who has come back to empty her dead or departed parents' house in a small Midwestern town the day before the sale closes
blueprint.addressee: The house itself (apostrophe), addressed as 'you' throughout
blueprint.situation: In 1957 the speaker tapes boxes and rolls rugs in the house her father built in 1931. As she goes, she remembers what the thick walls kept in: her father's violence toward her mother, which she covered as a child by turning up the radio. Tomorrow a young couple will move in and praise how quiet the house is.
blueprint.central_idea: The house's famous soundness, the thick walls that kept trouble in, matches the speaker's own lifelong habit of not hearing and not looking. Her calm departure without looking back is the same skill she learned at the radio dial.
blueprint.complexity: The speaker starts by half-accusing the house, a silent and complicit witness. Then she turns and admits that she was the one who turned the radio up. Her last boast, that she will not look back like Lot's wife, sounds like composure, but the poem has shown that this 'better' upbringing was training in concealment. So her refusal to look back is both a survival skill and a continuation of the harm.
blueprint.form_notes: Twenty-six lines of loose blank verse in five quatrains and a closing six-line stanza, with one clean closing rhyme (mat/that). The third stanza runs on into the fourth so that the reader moves straight from the walls into what they hid. The plain, wry diction of a mid-century domestic poem darkens into confession.
blueprint.setting: A plaster-and-joist house on Tenney Street in a small town, built 1931, emptied in 1957 before its sale; cellar furnace, creaking stair, front room, porch mat
characters: the speaker (adult daughter)
the house
the father (builder, implied abuser)
the mother
the real estate agent
the young buying couple with a baby
blueprint.conflict: Internal: the speaker's wish to blame the house and leave cleanly against her recognition of her own part in the family's silence

g-p01.title: To the House on Tenney Street, Before the Closing
g-p01.headnote: In this poem, the speaker addresses the house where she grew up on the day before it is sold.
stanzas: The agent calls you charming. She means old.
She means the stair that answers every foot,
the cellar where the furnace, like a bishop,
sits in its rusted robes and will not die.
I have taped the boxes, I have rolled the rugs
and found beneath them the pale squares of floor
the sun has never touched, as clean as the day
my father nailed the boards down in thirty-one.
You were a good house. Everyone said so.
Good plaster, good joists, a good tight roof
that kept the weather out and kept us in,
and walls so thick no neighbor ever heard
what you heard: the chair against the door,
my mother's voice going small, then smaller,
the radio turned up to cover it.
You held all that as a jar holds water.
But I was the one who turned the radio up.
I was eleven, and I knew the dial.
I knew which station had the loudest band.
So don't think I've come here to accuse you.
Tomorrow a couple up from Marlowe, with a baby,
will stand in your front room and praise the quiet.
They'll mean it as a compliment. I lock you,
slide the key beneath the mat, and walk
down to the car without once turning round.
Lot's wife looked back. I was raised better than that.

blueprint.speaker: A woman in her mid-thirties, born the year a rural branch line was dismantled, the daughter of a former track worker
blueprint.addressee: Her father, once a ganger on the line, now in a wheelchair at a care home called Fairholme
blueprint.situation: At her father's request she walks the eleven miles of the closed Kell Valley branch, from Ashby Halt to Corran, carrying his flask and map, supposedly to check the track keys at Dunmore cutting, though the rails were lifted decades ago
blueprint.central_idea: The errand is not a test of the father's failing memory but a way of lending him the walk his body can no longer make; the daughter's planned lie that the keys are holding becomes a loving support, like the small wooden key that holds a rail in place.
blueprint.complexity: The poem first seems to show a confused old man sending his daughter on a pointless task. At the volta the speaker realizes he knew all along, since he pulled the last keys himself. Pity turns into an unspoken understanding. The closing lie is both untrue and faithful: a fiction both of them accept, described in the language of track-building so that the poem praises a deception without being sentimental about it.
blueprint.form_notes: Five free-verse stanzas of uneven length (5, 6, 7, 8, 7 lines). Plain, concrete diction with railway vocabulary (keys, sleepers, cutting, ganger). Enjambment carries the walk forward. The volta sits in the middle of the fourth stanza and is marked by a colon and a caesura. The final stanza is one long sentence that settles into the closing metaphor.

characters: the speaker

blueprint.conflict: The gap between the father's errand and what is actually left of the line, and the speaker's choice between telling him the truth and telling him a kind lie

g-p02.title: Trackbed, Kell Valley Branch
g-p02.headnote: The following poem is by the contemporary poet Isla Brennick. The speaker walks the route of a railway branch line that closed many years earlier.
stanzas: "Walk it for me," you said, "the whole eleven,
Ashby Halt to Corran. And check the keys
at Dunmore cutting. They work loose in heat."
So here I am with your flask and your map,
folded so often the river has worn through.
The rails went for scrap the year I was born.
What's left is cinder laid across the fields
like a parting combed in a child's hair
the morning of a photograph. Cow parsley
up to my shoulder. A woman with a spaniel
nods as if I'd come to read the meter.
Milepost three. Milepost four, its numbers
rubbed bright by someone's thumb, or weather.
No sleepers either. They went for fences,
for raised beds, for the step outside the Drover's.
Of all the sleepers you are the last one
still on the line, in your chair at Fairholme,
brakes on, the television naming birds.
At Dunmore cutting there is nothing to tighten.
The walls sweat green. A wren goes off
like a dropped spanner, and the cold
comes up out of the stone, and I see it:
you knew. You pulled the last keys yourself
in nineteen eighty-three, with a bar and a curse.
What you have lost is not the map. It's the walk,
eleven miles, a sentence you can't finish.
So I finish it for you, at your pace,
the old one, a ganger's, eyes on the ground,
and tonight I'll tell you the keys are holding.
It's the kind of lie you taught me, the kind
a railway's made of: small, wooden, driven
hard into the gap to keep the heavy thing
from shifting while the weight goes over.

g-p03.title: The Bench in Vrana Square

provenance.note: Original poem in a mid-twentieth-century plain-spoken free-verse manner; invented author, village and characters.

g-p03.headnote: The following poem is by an invented writer, set in a small river village some years after a war.

blueprint.speaker: An adult grandson, educated in the city, who left the village in forty-nine and has come back after his grandfather's burial
blueprint.addressee: His dead grandfather, addressed directly as 'Grandfather' and 'you'
blueprint.situation: A month after the grandfather's burial, the village council is about to remove his bench from the square to make room for a glass bus shelter. The speaker sits on the bench and remembers the old man's daily vigil, which the whole village believed was kept only for Pavel, the son taken away by trucks in forty-two.
blueprint.setting: A village square with a fountain, the eastern road and the western city road, around 1961
characters: the speaker (grandson)
the grandfather
Pavel, the grandfather's son, taken in forty-two
the village women
the postman
the council
blueprint.central_idea: The grandson finds out that the vigil he scorned as a boy, which everyone took to be grief for a lost son, was also kept for him, the grandson who left and stopped writing. His adolescent shame turns into adult guilt.
blueprint.complexity: The poem is divided between public and private, past and present understanding. The village reveres the grandfather's grief and the boy despises his idleness, and both readings are partial. The worn west armrest shows a second, hidden waiting. So the speaker is both mourner and culprit, and the removal of the bench for a timetabled shelter sets the old man's open-ended faithfulness against a modern order the speaker himself chose.
blueprint.conflict: The speaker's guilt over his neglect against his earlier embarrassment, and the village's public story against the private evidence of the bench
blueprint.form_notes: Six unrhymed stanzas of plain, conversational free verse. Short declarative sentences and caesurae carry the confessions. Enjambment carries the memory and discovery. The poem turns in the fifth stanza at 'It is not at the fountain end' and closes on a three-line stanza ending in a stopped, confessional line.

stanzas: They are moving your bench on Thursday, Grandfather,
a month after they moved you up the hill,
to make room for a shelter the council voted,
glass on three sides, a timetable under glass.
Today it still stands where you bolted it down
the spring the river took the mill, its slats
gone gray as a mule's muzzle, one short leg
shimmed with a folded jack of clubs.
The whole square knew what you were doing there.
Mornings you took the end beside the fountain
and turned your hat-brim to the eastern road
the trucks had carried Pavel down in forty-two.
Like the old dog on the dung heap at Ithaca
who lived to know his master's step, you waited,
and the women crossing with their bread
lowered their voices, as if you were a church.
I was ashamed of you. I was fourteen.
I wanted a grandfather who mended nets
or lied about the war over plum brandy,
not one who sat all day like a stopped clock
and asked the postman, every noon, the same
two words, and thanked him for the answer.
In forty-nine I took the western bus
to the polytechnic and the city's
brick and neon, and I wrote at Easter,
then at Christmas, then I meant to write.
You never asked me why. You asked the postman.
Now I sit where you sat, and my hand
goes looking for the place your hand wore smooth.
It is not at the fountain end. It is
the other arm, rubbed pale as soap, the arm
that faces west, down the city road.
Afternoons, then, when the square had stopped
watching, you slid sideways down the slats to me.
On Thursday they will truck it to the depot.
The new bus will halt where your boots halted.
Twelve years I let you think the road was slow.

blueprint.speaker: Tom's widow, the mother of the boy, at a canal lock-keeper's house
blueprint.addressee: Her dead husband, Tom, the former lock-keeper
blueprint.situation: On an evening after tea, the widow watches her son stand on the lock-beam and whistle his dead father's tune. He gets as far as Tom always went, stops, and then makes up his own ending, which the boat drivers carry off along the towpath. In the last stanza she reveals that Tom never finished the tune because she used to sing its ending, and she chooses not to sing it now.
blueprint.central_idea: Loving the dead can mean holding back what they left you, so that the living can make something of their own. The widow's silence keeps the past in check, as a lock gate holds back water.
blueprint.complexity: Her silence is both possessive and generous. She keeps the true ending, the last private bond of her marriage, for herself, and in doing so she gives her son the freedom to finish the song his own way. The town will credit the boy with an ending that replaces hers, so her act is fidelity and self-erasure at once. Whether this is grief or love, she presents it without sentiment.
blueprint.form_notes: Five stanzas of loose blank verse, in the manner of a nineteenth-century domestic dramatic monologue. The first four stanzas flow into each other through enjambed stanza breaks (each of the first three ends on a comma or semicolon), which mimics the tune running on. The final stanza turns with a second apostrophe to Tom and ends on short, stopped sentences.

g-p04.title: The Upper Gate
g-p04.headnote: The following poem is a nineteenth-century-style piece by an invented poet. The speaker lives beside a canal lock.
stanzas: Tom, he has got your tune as far as you.
He stands upon the lock-beam after tea
and screws his mouth up sideways, as you did,
like one who blows the chaff from off his palm
to see what grain is left there; and it comes,
the first part clean, the second bending down,
and then the dry step in it where you'd stop
to knock your pipe out on the windlass post.
He stops there too. The water in the chamber
lifts its brown shoulder, waiting, as it waited
for every boat you ever let go down;
the heron on the far bank holds one foot.
I did not call to him. I had my reasons.
No Orpheus, he; he cannot whistle you
up out of Wendlecote churchyard with a tune,
and I would not have had him looking back.
He tries an ending. It is wrong. He tries
another, sharper, like a boy's new knife,
and that one holds. He whistles it again,
pleased with himself, again, until the coal-boats hear,
and the drivers drag it down the towpath with them,
his ending on your beginning, all the way
to Coldmere Locks, as if it had been so
since Adam. They will call it his by Sunday.
Tom, it was never for the want of notes
you stopped. You stopped because the rest was mine:
you whistled to the turn, and I sang down
the falling part across the drying-yard,
your shirts in my two arms. I have it still.
I keep it shut, the way you kept the gate
against the press of all the upper water,
and let his run downstream. I do not sing.

blueprint.addressee: No one at first (a general listener); in the final stanza the seed turns and addresses the dead farmer Teodor directly
blueprint.situation: Nine years into cold storage, the seed describes its nested enclosure, the twice-yearly inspection by a technician named Dagny, and its memory of the farmer who sealed its envelope. It then admits what its release would require.
blueprint.central_idea: Being preserved is not the same as living. The vault keeps the seed safe by keeping it from doing what it was made for, so its natural longing to grow can only come true through the disasters the vault exists to guard against.

g-p05.title: Accession 4471-B
g-p05.headnote: The following poem is by the contemporary poet Maren Oduya. The speaker is a seed held in long-term frozen storage.
stanzas: They tell me minus eighteen is a kindness.
I am a speckled bean from Teodor Halas's
upper field, the one that floods in April,
and I have slept inside a foil envelope
inside a box inside a mountain
for nine years, which is nothing, which is a breath.
Twice a year the light comes on. Dagny walks
the aisles in a coat as thick as a mattress,
reading the shelves like a teacher calling roll
in a school where nobody answers,
and goes out humming, and the dark shuts behind her.
Teodor wrote on our envelope in pencil:
good in poor ground. Do not let them dry out.
He licked the flap. I can still taste him,
salt and pipe smoke, a man who talked to rows
as if they might talk back. He has died since.
I know it the way we know a frost, without being told.
Down here I think about the girl
who ate six of our red cousins in the underworld
and had to stay below for half of every year.
At least they let her up for spring.
The mountain is patient. It has never wanted
anything, and it holds us the way a bank
holds a coin: to be worth something, never spent.
But I was made for one thing, which is splitting.
I practice it in my sleep. And what would open
the door for good is fire, or a war,
or the long drought they name in meetings,
the world above gone wrong enough
that someone needs me. So I am a prayer
that should not be answered. Forgive me, Teodor.
Some nights I want it so badly I almost crack.

blueprint.speaker: Miss Orrin, an unmarried woman lodging in a rented room above a coal merchant's near a railway line, shortly after a war in which her brother left by train
blueprint.addressee: No direct addressee; a private reckoning overheard by the reader, with the landlady Mrs. Pruett present in report and speech
blueprint.situation: From her window the speaker keeps a pencil tally of every passing train on the wallpaper. Her landlady brings water and gently teases her. Midway the speaker recalls her brother leaving on the six-ten one March, the one train she did not count; she now keeps an expired return ticket in her Bible and has counted four hundred and eleven trains.
blueprint.central_idea: Counting the trains looks like waiting to leave, but it is really a ritual of staying: a belated bookkeeping for the one departure she failed to mark, and a way of confirming that she herself remains.
blueprint.complexity: The speaker's tally is both devotion and evasion. It answers guilt over her brother's unmarked departure, yet it also lets her avoid the journey her ticket promises. The landlady reads her as someone about to go; the poem reveals she is both prisoner and warder of her own room. Precision becomes a form of grief, and departure-counting becomes proof of not departing.
blueprint.form_notes: Thirty-one lines in five unrhymed stanzas of loose blank verse. Three six-line stanzas of observation, a four-line stanza of memory that acts as the volta, and a longer final stanza that ends on a truncated four-word line. Enjambment carries the tally across lines; caesuras mark the clipped, factual voice.
blueprint.setting: A rented room above a coal merchant's on a street beside a rail line in an invented English-style junction town, around 1920; trains run to Harle and over the bridge at Corran.
characters: Miss Orrin, the speaker
Mrs. Pruett, her landlady
the speaker's brother, who left on the six-ten in March

g-p06.title: Room Above the Coal Merchant's
g-p06.headnote: The following poem is by an invented writer of the early twentieth century. The speaker lodges in a rented room beside a railway line.
stanzas: From the rented room above the coal merchant's
I count the trains. The nine-fourteen to Harle
goes by like a drawer pulled open in the dark
and shut again. I make a mark for it
in pencil on the wallpaper, by the bed,
where the roses have gone brown as tea.
Mrs. Pruett, bringing up the jug,
says, "Miss Orrin, you'll wear that window thin."
She means it kindly. She sets the water down
and does not ask what all the little gates are for,
the fives I bar across with one long stroke
like fences round a field where nothing grows.
Freight, mostly. Cattle, coal, and once a car
with one piano roped beneath a sheet,
bound for some parlor I will never sit in.
The night ones I count by ear: the long complaint
of the up-line, rails that talk in their sleep,
the bridge at Corran taking each in its teeth.
My brother went from here. The six-ten, March,
the window down, his cap held out, and then
the window empty. That one I did not count.
I did not know I was to keep the books.
Now I am thorough. Now I keep a ticket
folded in the Bible on the washstand,
Harle and back, third class, its date gone by.
Mrs. Pruett thinks I mean to go.
Four hundred and eleven, says the wall.
Not one of them has taken me. I count
the way a warder counts the cells at night,
not for the ones who leave, but to be sure
that I am here.

blueprint.setting: The Harlan Narrows cable ferry between Pell's Landing and Cutbank, a river crossing, October 1952 to March 1953
blueprint.situation: A woman whose husband has left town rides the ferry back and forth every Sunday all winter. The operator insists he does not care, but he keeps changing small habits for her. In March she gets off for good with a suitcase.
blueprint.conflict: The narrator's claimed indifference against his growing, unadmitted attention to Mrs. Lorne. Underneath that is the conflict between his fixed, repeating life and the possibility of leaving it, which she takes and he does not.
blueprint.central_idea: Going back and forth can be a way of putting off a decision. The woman who seems aimless uses it to make up her mind and then leaves. The man who carries other people to where they are going turns out to be the one with no destination.
blueprint.complexity: The narrator's denials ('it did not trouble me,' 'There was no call to') show the feeling they deny. The needle metaphor works both as a defense of steady work and as an admission of a life that never finishes anything. Mrs. Lorne's question about how many crossings he has made exposes his lie and suggests that she sees in him the stalled condition she is escaping. The ending puts his old routines back in place, but the reader now sees them as confinement.

g-s01.title: The Harlan Narrows Crossing
g-s01.headnote: The following passage is from a short story by Orrin Delacourt, set at a river crossing in the early 1950s.
paragraphs: The Harlan Narrows ferry runs on a cable, which is the first thing I tell people who ask whether it ever gets lost. It cannot get lost. Seven hundred yards of greased wire lie along the bottom from Pell's Landing to Cutbank, and the Ida Corley pulls herself along it like a woman feeling for the banister in the dark. Eleven minutes each way. I have run her since the spring of 1931, and in that time I have never once wondered where anybody was going. Wondering is for people on the bank.

Mrs. Lorne began in October of 1952. She paid her fifteen cents at Pell's, went to the upstream rail, and stood there with her pocketbook held against her stomach in both hands. At Cutbank the trucks rolled off and the feed-store man rolled off and she did not. She paid again. I took the money because it was money. By the fourth crossing the light on the water had gone the color of weak tea, and she was still at the rail, and I had stopped pretending to look at the gauge.

'You'll want to get off one side or the other,' I told her, round about the sixth trip. 'We tie up at seven.' 'I know when you tie up. It's on the sign.' 'There's nothing at Cutbank but the feed store and a church with no bell.' 'I've been to Cutbank,' she said, the way you'd say you'd been to the dentist. Then she asked how many times I had crossed, all told, and I said I had no idea, which was a lie. I had worked it out one winter on the back of a tide table, and it came to something over ninety thousand.

She came every Sunday after that, and I will say plainly that it did not trouble me. A passenger is a passenger. I did take to wiping down the upstream rail before the first run, but that was on account of the gulls, and if I kept the thermos of coffee on the bench instead of under it, that was only where it was handiest. I noticed her shoes were the same brown pair every week, resoled once in January. I noticed she never looked toward either landing, only at the water going under, as if she were reading it.

Lucille, who keeps the ticket booth at Pell's, said the woman was not right. Lucille said Mr. Lorne had gone to Detroit in the summer and sent back a postcard of a hotel. I said that was nobody's business. The way I see it, the Corley is a needle and the river is a hem that never gets finished, and a needle has no opinion about the cloth. It goes in and comes out. It goes in and comes out. A man could do worse than be a needle.

On the last Sunday in March she came aboard with a suitcase, a tan cardboard one with a strap buckled in the wrong hole. She set it by the rail and stood beside it and we crossed, and at Cutbank she picked it up. The ramp came down with its usual iron complaint. She stopped on the second plank. 'I wanted to see if it got easier, going over and over,' she said. 'It doesn't. It only gets the same.' She looked at me then, straight on, the first time since October. 'How many did you say, Mr. Ostrander?' 'I didn't say.' 'No,' she said. 'You didn't.'

She went up the road past the feed store toward where the county bus stops, and I hauled the ramp and took the Corley back to Pell's with nobody aboard, eleven minutes, the wire coming up dripping over the sheave and going down again behind. I did not watch the Cutbank side. There was no call to. When we tied up I wiped the upstream rail, out of habit, and put the thermos back under the bench where it belongs, and on Monday the trucks came the same as always and I took them where they were going.

g-s02.title: The Inner Wall
g-s02.headnote: The following passage is from a novel by the invented writer Harriet Moule, set in a small northern fishing port in the 1860s.

provenance.note: Original passage written in a 19th-century manner for practice use; writer, port, bank and characters are invented.

paragraphs: It was my duty in those years to sit at the lower end of the harbour-office table at Gullsend and write down whatever Captain Rendle said was so. I was nineteen, I wrote a clean round hand, and I believed that a thing entered in the Board's ledger had been, by that act, made true. On the morning I speak of, in November, the ledger lay open between us at a fresh page ruled in red, and the Captain had already written at its head: Quaile, Ezra, fisherman, seventy-one years, superannuated.

Old Quaile came in without knocking, much as the tide comes in, and stood dripping on the matting. He had been out since four. His jersey was stiff with salt, and his hands, which he offered to neither of us, hung at his sides like two ends of tarred rope left too long on the quay. The Captain rose, a thing I had never seen him do for a fisherman, and set a chair for him by the stove, where the coals were red and ticking.

'Sit down, Ezra. You'll take a drop of something against the cold.' 'I'll stand, Will. I've a catch going soft in the basket.' I had not known until that moment that the Captain possessed a Christian name which anybody used.

The Captain sat again and read from the paper before him. The Harbour Board, he said, in consideration of fifty-three years' unbroken service to the port, was pleased to settle upon Ezra Quaile the sum of seven shillings weekly for the term of his natural life, upon the sole condition that the lugger Providence vacate her berth at the inner wall, which berth was required for the accommodation of steam. He read it well. He had a voice for paper, the Captain, and the long words came off it smooth and pale as candles out of a mould.

Quaile did not look at him. He looked past him, through the salt-bleared window, at the inner wall, where the old luggers lay nose to the stones like cattle waiting at a gate, and where, beyond them, the two new drifters sat low and black and breathing smoke into the morning. The harbour had grown a second skyline that autumn, all funnels, and it did not smell of fish.

'The Board,' he said at last. 'I mind the Board. The Board had my brother's boat off his widow for the dues, the winter he went down in her. The Board never gave away a herring it hadn't counted twice.' He turned his cap in his hands. 'Who's paying it, Will?' The Captain coloured to the ears. 'The Board,' he said. 'Aye,' said Quaile, and looked, not at him, but at me, at my pen above the red-ruled page. 'Then write that down, lad, if it's so.'

I dipped my pen and did not write. Nobody spoke. The coals ticked. Quaile set his cap on, and when he spoke again it was gentler, which was worse. 'I learned thee to bait a long-line on that wall, the year thy father drank the rent. I'll not be paid for it now by the week, like a man that's lost a leg. Give my berth to the steam when I'm under, and welcome.' Then he went out to his basket, and we heard his boots go down the stone steps, unhurried, and the door swing to behind him on its weight.

The Captain stood a long while at the window. 'Write declined,' he said, without turning; and then, 'There is a draft in the drawer, Hobb, on the Penrock bank. You may put it in the stove.' I took it out. It was drawn on his own account, in his own hand, for a sum that would have paid seven shillings a week for many years, and the Board's name was nowhere on it. I burned it as I was told. But I have kept that page of the ledger, ruled in red, with the one word on it in my clean round hand; and it has taken me most of my life to see that it was the only true entry I ever made in that book, and that it was not my writing that made it so.

characters: Thomas Hobb, the narrator, recalling himself at nineteen as clerk of the harbour office
Captain Will Rendle, harbour master, once taught the fishing trade by Quaile
Ezra Quaile, a seventy-one-year-old fisherman, owner of the lugger Providence
blueprint.setting: The harbour office at Gullsend, an invented northern fishing port, on a November morning in the 1860s, as steam drifters begin to crowd out the old sailing luggers
blueprint.situation: The harbour master reads Quaile a pension offer, supposedly from the Board, on condition that his boat give up her berth to steam. Quaile suspects the money is the Captain's own, refuses it, and leaves. The Captain has the clerk write 'declined' and burn a private bank draft.
blueprint.conflict: Quaile's pride and his distrust of the Board against the Captain's disguised wish to repay a personal debt (and perhaps also to clear the berth). Underneath is the young clerk's faith in the written record against what the record leaves out.
blueprint.speaker: First-person retrospective narrator, an older man looking back at an interview he recorded as a young clerk
blueprint.central_idea: Official language and written record cannot turn a personal debt into a public favour. An old man's refusal keeps a truth that the ledger was meant to cover over.
blueprint.complexity: The Captain's offer is both kindness and convenience: he pays from his own pocket, but the condition still clears the berth for steam. Quaile's refusal is pride, loyalty and a judgment on the Board all at once. The narrator's opening faith that writing makes things true is overturned at the end. The one true entry, 'declined', is true because of Quaile's act, not because it was written.

g-s03.title: Canon One
g-s03.headnote: The following passage is from a contemporary short story. The narrator works as a professional interpreter.
paragraphs: The hospice called the agency at eleven on a Tuesday, and the agency called me, because I am the only Portuguese interpreter in Halsey County who will drive in snow. Room 14 at Saint Brendan's faced the parking lot and, past it, the gray chop of the harbor, where the trawlers sat frozen to their moorings like plates left overnight in a sink.

Mr. Aurelio Furtado was ninety pounds of man under a blanket the color of weak tea. His daughter stood by the radiator with her coat still zipped. She was perhaps fifty, with his long jaw, and she held out three sheets of lined paper folded into a square so small it looked as if it had been carried in a shoe. "He wrote it last month," she said. "Before. He wants it read to me while he can still hear it." She paused. "I don't speak it. I never did. He made sure of that."

Behind my badge, on the same lanyard, I keep a laminated card with the code of ethics. Canon one: render the message faithfully, without addition, omission, or distortion. I have held to it in depositions and emergency rooms, through a woman's miscarriage and a roofer's drunk-driving plea. The oxygen concentrator beside the bed took its long breaths for him and let them out with a small complaint, as if it, too, had been asked to work past its hours.

I unfolded the letter. His was the handwriting of the island schools of seventy years ago, every capital a little ship under sail. The first page was easy. "Dana," I read, "I am writing this because my mouth was never good for it." He wrote about the house on Rua da Pena, the fig tree that split the cistern, the boat he had named for her grandmother and then sold. Dana kept her arms folded. The English came out of me clean and plain, and I could hear each sentence land on her and stay.

The second page was why he left. In Portuguese the sentence was short. I went because I was happy with Lurdes in a way I was never happy in your mother's kitchen, and I would go again. I looked at it long enough that Dana unfolded her arms. Faithfully, the card said. Without omission. Without distortion. The concentrator sighed. Out in the lot a plow went back and forth across the same stretch of asphalt, scraping it bare, scraping it bare.

"I went because I was afraid," I read. "Afraid of the kitchen, afraid of being a father in a language I did not have. I was a coward, and I would give anything to go back." Dana's mouth did something it had not decided to do. She sat on the edge of the bed carefully, the way you sit on ice you don't trust.

The third page I read nearly as he wrote it: the account at the Halsey Credit Union; his watch, which was to go to a grandson he had met twice; a request that they not bury him in a suit. Dana laughed at the suit, once, wetly, and put her hand on the blanket where his knee was. My voice was a borrowed coat, and I was handing it back with something left in the pocket.

When I finished, Mr. Furtado's eyes were open. They found me, not her. "Não foi isso que eu escrevi," he said, in a voice like a page turning. That is not what I wrote. "Eu sei," I said. I know. Dana looked up from his knee. "What did he say?" The plow had stopped. Under my badge the card lay flat against my chest. "He says I read it well," I told her, and her father closed his eyes, and whatever crossed his face on the way down, I have not been able to name it.

characters: Clemency (Clemmie) Venn-type narrator: the clockmaker's daughter, about thirty, a governess-teacher at Corlett Hall for eleven years

blueprint.setting: A clockmaker's shop in Salter's Row, Marlbury Hythe, an English market town, March 1913; one day and night after the father's death
blueprint.situation: The daughter comes home to sell her father's shop and finds all forty-one clocks stopped at different hours. A neighbor tells her the father stopped them himself after she left. She finds her letters with hours pencilled on them that match the stopped clocks, but she will not make the connection. She winds the clocks, can't sleep, and at midnight stops them again.
blueprint.conflict: Internal: the narrator's settled resentment of a father she thinks was indifferent, set against evidence that he grieved her absence; external in small: her verdict against Fenwick's silent disagreement.
blueprint.central_idea: A daughter who insists she is unsentimental and her father was indifferent ends up taking on his grief along with his trade. She repeats his act of stopping time while denying what that act meant.
blueprint.complexity: The narrator's practical voice is both a defense and a sign of the same temperament as her father's; the evidence she reports (labels, letters, matching hours, Fenwick's silence) exceeds her conclusions; the ending both echoes and departs from the father (she stops the clocks but refuses to record the hour), leaving open whether this is reconciliation or a sharper refusal.

g-s04.title: The Regulator
g-s04.headnote: The following passage is from a novel by Edith Marrable, published in 1921 and set in an English market town.
paragraphs: My father died on a Tuesday in March of 1913, and on the Friday I came home to Marlbury Hythe to sell his shop. I will say at once that I am not a sentimental woman. Eleven years of teaching other people's daughters their French verbs at Corlett Hall had seen to that. I had the key from the solicitor in my glove and a list in my head, and I meant to be on the four-fifteen train by Monday.

The shop in Salter's Row was as I had left it, only quieter. Forty-one clocks hung or stood about the walls, and not one of them was going. They had stopped at all hours: the bracket clock at ten past two, the pair of carriage clocks at a quarter to nine and twenty to six, the great long-case by the window, which had the patient face of a creditor, at four exactly. The room seemed to hold every hour of the day at once and to live in none of them. The silence was thick as felt. Outside, the carts ground over the setts toward the market and a boy was crying herring; inside, the dust lay on the bench in an even grey, like snow nobody had walked on.

When I was a girl he kept them all running. On Sunday evenings he wound them in a fixed order, the regulator first and the little painted cuckoo last, and I was set on the high stool to say my catechism while he worked. He timed me by the regulator. 'Time is a debt, Clemmie,' he told me once, without lifting his eyeglass. 'Every tick is a penny paid out.' I took it, at nine years old, to mean that I was costing him. He never once looked up from the bench when I spoke; I am quite sure of that.

Mr. Fenwick, the ironmonger from next door, came in at eleven with his hat in both hands. He offered eight pounds for the lot, which was robbery, and I told him so. Then he stood looking at the long-case as though it might speak up for him. 'He stopped them himself, miss, one and another, after you went away,' he said. 'Said he couldn't abide the counting.' 'He was ill,' I said. 'Or idle. In a tradesman it comes to the same.' Mr. Fenwick turned his hat a quarter-turn, like a man setting a dial, and said nothing at all, which in Marlbury Hythe is a kind of argument.

When he had gone I took the keys from the drawer. Each was tied with a paper label in my father's small, sloping hand, naming its clock, as though the clocks were lodgers he was obliged to keep account of. Beneath the keys lay my letters, all eleven years of them, in order, and on every envelope he had pencilled an hour: 2.10, 8.45, 5.40, and on the last, which told him I should not be home that Christmas either, 4.0. He was a man who noted things. It means nothing more than that.

I wound every one. It took the better part of the afternoon. I set them by the church, which is three minutes fast and always has been, and started each pendulum with my finger, and by five o'clock the room was full of them: forty-one small industries ticking out of step, the long-case slow and grave, the carriage clocks hurrying like clerks late for the office. It was exactly the sound of being nine years old. I ate my supper standing up, among them.

I did not sleep. The ticking came up through the boards as it had when I was a child, counting, counting, and at midnight I went down in my wrapper with the candle. A stopped clock fetches the same at auction as a going one; any dealer will tell you so, and I had a train to catch. I stopped them one by one, the regulator first. I left the long-case for last. It was a quarter past twelve when I put my finger to its pendulum, and I did not write the hour down.

characters: Emil, the narrator: sixteen in 1931, apprenticed to a watchmaker, telling the story as a grown man who now owns a shop
Anton Pruss, a watchmaker on Ferry Street who never bills Mrs. Valk
Mrs. Valk, a widow who keeps bringing in her dead husband's gold watch with the mainspring overwound
blueprint.setting: Calder Falls, a river town, in February 1931: a watch shop full of ticking on Ferry Street, and a cold, stripped house at the top of Orchard Street
blueprint.situation: Emil delivers Mrs. Valk's watch after its third repair. In her emptied house he sees a mantel clock with its pendulum tied still, and through the window he watches her overwind the watch. He reports this to Pruss, who answers that she pays by bringing it back.
blueprint.conflict: Emil's view that everything is a debt to be counted runs against Pruss's quiet forbearance and against Mrs. Valk's grief. The older narrator still insists he is not soft, but what he did contradicts him.
blueprint.central_idea: A debt that is never collected can be a kind of loyalty. The repair-and-undoing cycle keeps the widow's grief going, and the narrator, without admitting it, ends up keeping the cycle going himself.
blueprint.complexity: The narrator is partly unreliable. He reports details that point to grief (bare walls, the tied pendulum, the winding) but reads them as a trick. The Penelope allusion works against his reading. The ending shows him burning a bill and rationalizing it, so he has taken on Pruss's mercy while still talking like a bookkeeper. Time also matters: the shop's 'disagreeing' clocks against the house's stopped one.

g-s05.title: The Hunter Case
g-s05.headnote: The following passage is from a short story published in 1956. The narrator recalls a winter he spent as apprentice to a watchmaker.
paragraphs: In the winter of 1931 I was sixteen and bound for three years to Anton Pruss, who kept a watch shop on Ferry Street in Calder Falls, between a bakery and a dentist who did not believe in gas. The shop ticked. Forty clocks on the walls and a hundred watches in the drawers went each its own small way, so that standing among them was like standing in a rain that could not agree with itself. Mr. Pruss could hear a sick escapement across the room. I heard only rain, and money in it, every tick a cent somebody owed us.

Mrs. Valk's watch came in for the third time that February. It was a gold hunter that had been her husband's, with a crack across the crystal she would not let us replace, and each time it arrived the mainspring had been wound past bearing, wound until it gave. Mr. Pruss fitted a new spring without a word, cleaned the works, set it to the minute, and laid it in a twist of tissue. 'Take it up to her, Emil.' He never sent a bill. I had kept the day book since Christmas, and I knew what Mrs. Valk owed to the penny, which was eleven dollars and forty cents, and what she had paid, which was nothing at all.

Orchard Street climbed away from the river in a series of shelves, and her house sat on the highest one, its porch roof sagging like a tired lip. Somebody had shoveled half the walk and stopped. I rang, and waited, and rang, and the bell went off somewhere deep in the house the way a cough goes off in an empty church.

She was small and wore a man's cardigan over her dress, the sleeves turned back twice. The hall was colder than the porch. It smelled of kerosene and of apples gone soft in a cellar, and on the wallpaper were pale oblongs where pictures had hung, clean as windows. On the parlor mantel stood a clock with its pendulum tied to the case by a length of black ribbon. I thought: she cannot keep a clock going, and she means to keep a watch.

She took the tissue from me and unwrapped it on her palm and opened the case and held the watch to her ear. 'It's going,' she said, as though I had brought news of a death. She did not offer to pay and I did not ask; Mr. Pruss had forbidden it. She offered me tea instead. I said the shop was busy. It was not busy. Going down the walk I looked back through the parlor window, and she was sitting under the tied clock with the watch in both hands, winding it, and winding it, and winding it.

I was not a fool. We had read in school about Penelope, who, while her husband was away, unpicked by night what she wove by day so the suitors would go on waiting, and I took the story for what I thought it was, a trick, a woman's way of getting something without paying its price. I walked back down Orchard Street composing what I would say to Mr. Pruss, and by the bottom of the hill it was very fine.

He was at the bench with the loupe in his eye, and he did not take it out. I told him she broke the watch on purpose. I told him she sat and wound it till the spring let go, and that she would do it again. 'Yes,' he said. 'She'll bring it Tuesday week, I should think.' I said she owed eleven dollars and forty cents. 'She pays,' he said. I asked him in what. He turned a screw a quarter of a turn, and the shop went on ticking around us, forty clocks not agreeing, and then he said, 'She brings it back.'

I have had my own shop on Ferry Street for twenty years now, and I send bills, and people pay them. I am not soft. But I will set down that I wrote Mrs. Valk a bill myself that spring, in my best hand, eleven dollars and forty cents, and that I put it in the stove, which I tell myself was because a stamp cost two cents and she was not worth the stamp.

characters: VERA HOLLIS, fifties, keeper of the Gannet House, whose daughter marries tomorrow
THE STRANGER (WALT PELL), her husband, who left the family eighteen years earlier
blueprint.setting: The front desk of the Gannet House, a narrow hotel in the lake town of Port Ellery, near midnight in late May, early 1950s; paper wedding bells hang from the light fixture.
blueprint.situation: A traveler with a cardboard suitcase asks for a room in a hotel full of wedding guests. He raises his offer bill by bill while the keeper refuses, until she names a price of twelve dollars and calls him by name. She has known him from the moment he shut the door.
blueprint.conflict: Walt wants some place, however small, at his daughter's wedding; Vera wants to protect the day and refuses him the standing of family, yet she cannot quite turn him away.
blueprint.central_idea: Money stands in for an obligation that can never be paid; Vera can let Walt in only as a paying stranger, so that her concession and her refusal turn out to be the same act.
blueprint.complexity: Vera's refusal is real and so is her tenderness: she remembers his habit with the door and echoes it at the end, she gives him her daughter's old room, and she keeps his money for the wedding rather than the till. Walt asks for little, 'only' to see the bride, but his last question shows that he hopes for more. Even the reckoning is done in the language of a hotel bill.

devices.quote: The house is asleep.
devices.function: Vera's closing line repeats Walt's old habit of treating the house as a sleeper, so intimacy surfaces even as she dismisses him.

devices.quote: It's eighteen years at nothing a year, Walt.
devices.function: Turns the price of the room into a bill for his years of absence and recasts the haggling as a reckoning.

devices.quote: she lays it face down without looking up
devices.function: The photograph stands for the family life Vera guards; turning it face down and face up again shows her ambivalence.

devices.quote: He eases the door shut so it will not bang.

devices.quote: Five dollars is a fair price for a full house.
devices.function: Walt haggles as if over a room when the real cost is far greater, irony the audience feels once his identity comes out.

g-l01.headnote: The following scene is from The Kitchen Room, a play by Ruth Abernathy Kell, set in a small lake-town hotel in the early 1950s.
g-l01.title: The Kitchen Room
paragraphs: (The front desk of the Gannet House, a narrow hotel in Port Ellery. Near midnight, late May. A radiator knocks, though the season is long past needing it. Paper bells hang crooked from the light fixture. Behind the desk VERA HOLLIS, fifties, writes in a ledger. A framed photograph stands at her elbow; when the street door opens, she lays it face down without looking up. The STRANGER enters: a man about her age, a cardboard suitcase, a good hat gone soft at the brim. He eases the door shut so it will not bang.)
STRANGER. Evening. I'd like a room.
VERA. We're full. There's a wedding.
STRANGER. So I saw. Bells on the door, bells on the lamp. Somebody in this town owns a lot of crepe paper. (He sets the suitcase down as if it lives there.) One night. I don't need a view.
VERA. Nobody gets a view. The lake's on the other side of the cannery. (She turns a page.) The Lindqvist place on Water Street might have a cot.

STRANGER. I tried the Lindqvist place. They've got the groom's people stacked in the parlor like cordwood. (He takes out a wallet and lays a bill on the open ledger.) I'm in pumps. Sump pumps, well pumps. I go where the water is.
VERA. (She slides the bill off the ledger with the end of her pen, as if it might stain the page.) Then go to the lake.
STRANGER. Five dollars is a fair price for a full house. (Another bill.) Seven is generous.
VERA. Seven is what my rooms cost in August, with breakfast. It's May. I'm full.
STRANGER. Everybody has a room they don't count. A sewing room. A room where the roof leaks and the bed's got one short leg. (A third bill.) Ten. I'll sleep on the short side.

VERA. (She opens the drawer of keys. She does not take one out. She closes it.) There's a room over the kitchen. The stovepipe runs through it. It's hot as a mouth till four in the morning. (He waits.) It was my daughter's room. She's in the good front room tonight, with her dress hung on the closet door so it won't crease. Tomorrow she's somebody's wife, and the kitchen room goes back to being nobody's. (Pause.) Twelve dollars.
STRANGER. (Slowly he counts out two more bills. His hand stays on them.) Twelve. That's a funny number.
VERA. It's eighteen years at nothing a year, Walt. I rounded down.
WALT. (He takes off his hat at last. The radiator knocks twice and goes quiet.) When did you know?

VERA. When you shut the door so it wouldn't bang. You always did that. Like the house was asleep and you were the only one decent enough to let it be. (She turns the photograph up, looks at it, lays it face down again.) Pumps.
WALT. I was in pumps. For a while. (Beat.) I only want to see her walk in. I'd sit in the last pew and nobody would turn around.
VERA. Everybody turns around at a wedding. That's what the aisle is for.
WALT. Then I'll stand outside and watch the doors.
VERA. (She dips her pen and writes in the ledger, carefully, as for any guest.) Name.
WALT. You know my name.

VERA. I know what it was. (She writes.) W. Pell. Pumps. One night. (She takes a key from the drawer and lays it on the money, not in his hand.) The back stairs. Breakfast is at six for family. You're not family. The bus to Carrow leaves at seven-ten.
WALT. (He picks up the key and leaves the money where it lies.) And if I miss the bus?

VERA. Then you'll be one more man in this town who missed something. (She closes the ledger.) Mind the door going up. The house is asleep. (He goes. She sits a long while. She turns the photograph over and looks at it; then she squares the bills into a stack and puts them, not in the till, but in the pocket of her apron, the one that holds the pins for tomorrow's hem.)

g-l02.title: The Inspector of the Second Circle
g-l02.headnote: The following passage is from a novel by Ottilie Varga-Brenner, published in 1868. The narrator is the aging schoolmaster of Brusk, a hill village in a central European province.

provenance.note: Original passage written for practice; author, places and institutions are invented.

paragraphs: The letter from the Ministry gave the hour as ten, and so by eight I had the children washed, the stove raked, and the inkwells filled to a uniform height, which I tested with a straw. I read the signature three times before I believed it: Dr. E. Strand, Inspector of the Second Circle. There is only one Strand in Brusk, and he grinds our barley; and there was only ever one Strand boy who learned his declensions faster than I could set them.

I remember him at nine years old, standing on the bench by the window because he was too small to see the map, his finger pressed on Hallerstadt as if he meant to keep it from sliding off the paper. It was I who walked down to the mill and told his father the boy was wasted on sacks. It was I who wrote to the Gymnasium. I do not say this to claim him. I say it because it was true, and because on that morning I said it to myself a good many times, as a man pats his pocket to be sure of a coin.

He came up the lane at a quarter to ten in a hired gig, which the hill did not like; the horse stopped twice to consider it. He wore grey, and spectacles, and the reasonable sort of beard that men grow in offices. When I put out my hand he took it, and then he drew off his glove and took it again, as though the first had been a draft that wanted correcting.

"You are well, Herr Lehrer?" he said. Not my name; my title. I thought: he is shy before the children, he will not seem to presume. The children stood when he entered, all nineteen, with a scraping like geese leaving water, and Liesl Haber, whom I had drilled in the rivers of the province, began upon the Kett before anyone had asked her.

He did not ask her anything. He took from his coat a brass rule that folded upon itself in six joints, opened it with a small clicking, and measured the windows. He measured the ceiling by standing on my chair. He measured from the stove to the farthest bench, and wrote the figure in a book bound in green cloth. All the while my own rod of ash hung on its nail beside the stove, where it had hung for twenty-two years, and where, I may say, it had not once been taken down for him.

"The stove smokes," he observed. "It has always smoked," I said. "You used to say it kept off the wolves." This was a joke between us, or had been. He wrote something down. The stove, as if to oblige him, put out a grey tongue from under its lid and licked the ceiling he had measured.

He asked Anton Rusk to divide seven hundred by twelve, and Anton, who can tell the weight of a pig at a glance, wept. "They are frightened of the Ministry," I said. "Yes," he said gently. "That is noted also."

At noon, when the children had gone down to their soup, he folded the brass rule joint by joint and told me that the school at Brusk would be joined at Martinmas to the school at Ober-Kett, where there was a proper building, and a master trained in the new method, and a stove that drew. The Ministry had been pleased to accept the Inspector's recommendation. He did not look at the rod on its nail. He looked at me, and I saw in his face the very expression he had worn at the map, as if he meant to keep something from sliding off. "You taught me, sir," he said, "that we do not love a thing by lying about its size."

I had said it, I suppose. I have said a great many things in that room. I walked him down to the gig, and I held the horse's head while he climbed in, as I would have done for anyone from the Ministry.

characters: The narrator, the aging schoolmaster of Brusk, proud and anxious
Dr. Emil Strand, his former star pupil, now Inspector of the Second Circle
Liesl Haber and Anton Rusk, village pupils
blueprint.setting: A one-room hill-village school in Brusk, in an invented central European province, on the morning of an inspection; mid-nineteenth century
blueprint.situation: The schoolmaster prepares for a visit from the Ministry and finds that the inspector is the miller's son he once sent to the city; the inspector measures the room, briefly tests the children, and announces that the school will be merged on his own recommendation.
blueprint.conflict: The schoolmaster's wish to be recognized and vindicated by the pupil he made, set against Strand's duty to judge the school impersonally; internally, the narrator's pride against his half-admitted sense of being displaced.
blueprint.central_idea: A teacher's success can come back to him as a judgment against him: the pupil he formed applies the master's own lesson in honesty to close the master's school, and pride and loss become one thing.
blueprint.complexity: Strand is neither villain nor ingrate; his formality conceals regard (the corrected handshake, the childhood expression at the map), and his verdict rests on the narrator's own teaching. The narrator protests that he does not claim the boy while claiming him, explains away signs of distance, and at the end answers formality with formality. The unused rod (favor, personal authority) is set against the brass rule (impersonal measurement), which records everything except the room's history.

blueprint.setting: The lounge of the Ostrander Curling Club in a small Manitoba town, a winter afternoon, the funeral reception; a window looks out on sheet three, where the rings are painted beneath the ice.
blueprint.situation: After their father's funeral, the narrator and Owen sit across a folding table and say nothing to each other while their aunt talks and the mourners drift away.
blueprint.conflict: The narrator blames Owen for staying away during their father's dying, but his own list of grievances shows he did not call Owen until after the death; beneath this is a rivalry for the father's approval and a bond neither brother will put into words.
blueprint.central_idea: Silence between family members can carry both grievance and love; the brothers' refusal to speak is itself the wordless language their father taught them.
blueprint.complexity: The first-person narrator claims indifference ('I did not look at him once') while recording Owen in close detail; he builds a case against Owen that undoes itself (the late phone call); the father's silence, which might look cold, was a code that held the family together, and Owen's double tap at the end revives it. The painted house under the ice, which 'would not move,' stands for a bond the narrator says he 'used to' believe in. A strong essay would discuss the irony of the narrator's self-portrait, the contrast of Bernice's empty talk with meaningful silence, and the ending's ambiguous answer, a palm held flat.

g-l03.title: from The Hog Line
g-l03.headnote: The following passage is from The Hog Line, a 2019 novel by Marnie Halvorsen. The narrator and his brother attend the reception after their father's funeral in a small Manitoba town.
paragraphs: The reception was in the lounge of the Ostrander Curling Club because the Legion had a leak, and because my father had spent more of his life in this room than in our house, though nobody said that part out loud. Aunt Bernice had laid out the ham in the shape of a fan. There were squares, the lemon kind and the kind with coconut, and a coffee urn that clicked to itself as if it were counting the mourners. My brother Owen sat across the folding table from me. I did not look at him once.

I can tell you he wore a navy suit too good for Ostrander, the kind that does not shine at the knees, and that he had driven the eleven hours from Calgary without stopping, because his car was still ticking in the lot when I came out of the church. I can tell you he took two pickles and ate neither. He turned a new watch on his wrist when Mrs. Pankiw said he was the image of Dad, which he is not. I am the one with Dad's hands. Everyone has always said so.

Bernice talked for both of us. She talked like a kettle, steadily and to no one, about the casserole dish she would want back and the minister who had said Leonard instead of Lenny and how the snow had held off, God love it, held off just for him. "You boys," she said, and put a hand on each of our shoulders, so that for a moment she was a bridge with a car stalled at either end. "You boys eat." We ate.

Behind Owen the big window looked onto sheet three, where Gord Sawchuk was pebbling the ice for the evening draw, walking backward with the tank on his back and shaking the water out in a fine hiss. Under the ice the house was painted, red ring and white ring and blue, the button in the middle. It had been painted there before either of us was born. You could skate over it, sweep over it, drop a forty-pound stone on it, and it would not move. I used to think that was the whole point of a house.

Dad skipped our rink for six winters, Owen at lead and me at second, and he could not stand a man who talked on the ice. He called the game with his broom and his hands. A flat palm meant hold. A finger tapped twice meant sweep, hard, now, and I would see Owen's broom going before mine was off the pebble, and Dad at the far end with his face giving nothing, his whole body leaning after a rock he could not touch. The year Owen was fifteen we lost the final to the Kowalchuk sisters. Dad said nothing for forty miles of the drive home and then said, "Good weight, Owen," and that was the end of it. I don't remember what he said to me. I'm sure it was something.

Around four the Pankiws left, then the minister, then the church ladies with their foil. Bernice started stacking cups. Owen stood and buttoned his good jacket, and I thought, fine, that's it, eleven hours there and eleven back, and I lined up everything I would have said to him: the cot by Dad's bed at the regional hospital, the bedpans, the nine mornings Dad asked for him by name and I said he was on his way, and the call I finally made on the tenth. I had it all lined up like stones along the boards, waiting to be thrown.

He didn't say goodbye. He reached across the table, past the wrecked fan of ham, and with one finger he tapped the wood twice beside my plate. Then he went out to the lot. I sat there. On sheet three Gord had finished, and the pebble was setting, and the house lay under it the way it always had. It was a while before I noticed my own hand flat on the table, palm down, holding.
